The Nigerian Guild of Editors has called on relevant authorities to reopen the investigation into the assassination of renowned journalist, Dele Giwa, insisting that the passage of 40 years must not end the quest for justice. Giwa, a co-founder of Newswatch magazine, was killed by a parcel bomb delivered to his home on October 19, 1986. Four decades after the incident, no one has been brought to justice for his murder. The Guild made the call in a statement on Monday, jointly signed by its President, Eze Anaba, and General Secretary, Onuoha Ukeh, to mark the 40th anniversary of Giwa’s assassination. The NGE described the unresolved case as a painful test of Nigeria’s commitment to press freedom, public accountability and the rule of law, warning that it should not be allowed to fade into history. “Forty years is a long time to wait for justice. It is an unconscionably long time for a nation that claims to uphold the rule of law,” the Guild stated. The editors’ body urged the appropriate authorities to revisit the case, examine any credible evidence still available, preserve relevant records and pursue every lawful avenue towards establishing the circumstances surrounding Giwa’s death. The editors’ forum, however, cautioned against trial by media, stressing that its demand was not for anyone to be condemned without evidence but for a credible investigation into what it described as a grave crime against a journalist and press freedom. “We are not calling for trial by media. We are not asking anyone to be condemned without evidence. Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. The editors said the failure to resolve the murder raised questions about the country’s commitment to protecting journalists and holding perpetrators of attacks against media practitioners accountable. They also warned that the unresolved assassination could send a troubling message to journalists investigating corruption, probing abuses of power or exposing the activities of influential interests. The NGE added that the responsibility to investigate serious crimes did not expire with the passage of time or changes in political leadership. “An unresolved murder is not a closed chapter. It is an open wound in the nation’s conscience,” the guild said. 40 years after, NGE demands justice for Dele Giwa Dele Giwa: Doctor recalls final moments, MRA demands justice Christiane Amanpour to leave CNN after 43 years Beyond demanding justice, the editors used the anniversary to reflect on the state of journalism in Nigeria, urging practitioners to uphold independence, accuracy, fairness and professional ethics. They described Giwa as a journalist of uncommon courage, intellectual rigour and literary elegance, who demonstrated that journalism could challenge those in authority while maintaining high professional standards. According to the statement, Giwa understood that journalism was neither a public relations department for those in power nor an instrument for flattering the powerful, but a public trust. The statement noted that Giwa’s assassination was not merely the killing of an individual but an attack on the freedom to ask questions, expose wrongdoing and hold public officials accountable. The Guild also urged editors to protect newsroom integrity, publishers to resist intimidation and journalists to maintain professional discipline amid disinformation, political propaganda, economic pressures and the growing misuse of social media. “Courage without accuracy can become recklessness; independence without ethics can become irresponsibility,” it said, adding that journalism worth defending must be both fearless and scrupulous, independent and accountable. The NGE further called on public authorities to tolerate scrutiny and security agencies to protect journalists from threats and attacks, stressing that press freedom required more than constitutional guarantees. The Guild stated that the protection of journalists must be supported by responsible journalism, independent media institutions and effective enforcement of laws. It also cautioned against reducing Giwa’s memory to annual commemorations without concrete efforts to address the circumstances of his death. It urged journalism schools and newsrooms to teach and discuss Giwa’s professional ideals, while calling on younger journalists to appreciate the sacrifices made by earlier generations in defending the profession. “A parcel bomb may have ended Dele Giwa’s life, but it could not extinguish the ideals he represented. “Dele Giwa is gone, but the questions his murder left behind remain alive. The man was silenced; the search for justice must not be,” the statement concluded.
